To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
parents and teachers have a range of perceptions about the purposes of national assessment, which are not always consistent with each other or with the official purposes as stated by the government.

(1) the introduction of national assessment has had a significant impact on parents’ perceptions of the purpose of education, and their expectations of the education system and of their own children; (2) the impact of assessment on parents is mediated by their own attitudes to schooling, and the extent of their involvement in their children’s education; (3) parents are more concerned with the quality of their children’s education than the quantity of the information they receive about it; (4) parents’ perceptions of
the introduction of SATs at Key Stage One has led to a significant shift in the balance of assessment from teacher‐ to test‐based assessment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of assessment on parents and teachers and with the impact of assessment procedures on classroom practice.
the effects of assessment on parents, teachers, children and their learning in primary schools.

the SATs have not had the effect of improving the quality of teaching and learning, and have had little impact on the way in which teachers and schools operate.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the SATs were not perceived as being of value to the children by the parents, that they were seen as having a negative influence on teaching and learning, and that their introduction has had a negative impact on the relationships between parents and teachers.
the SATs had a positive effect in that they provided a stimulus for teachers to develop more systematic and explicit approaches to assessment.
the introduction of standardized assessment at Key Stage 1 in 1991 has had a number of effects on the children and the parents of Key Stage 1 children in England.
The main takeaway from our work is that
teachers and parents have very different ideas of what constitutes a good school.
the SATs have a profound effect on the way that teachers and schools approach assessment and on their relationships with the parents.
teachers and parents have very different perceptions of the effects of assessment on children’s learning, with teachers being more likely than parents to believe that assessment is beneficial.
